steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting InfiMM-HD, a multimodal large language model for high-resolution image understanding. It should explain how current MLLMs bridge vision encoders and LLMs, why high resolution is hard, how our architecture and multi-stage training address it, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- MLLMs: vision encoders + LLMs, emergent abilities
- Vision-language bridging modules: two aspects
- Transformation/alignment: Perceiver-Resampler/Q-Former vs MLP
- Integration: cross-attention vs concatenation
- Low resolution problem and cost of higher resolution
- InfiMM-HD architecture and four-stage training
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- MLLMs
  - pretrained vision encoders + LLMs (cite)
  - Flamingo (cite), BLIP-2 (cite), LLaVA (cite), MiniGPT-4 (cite) etc.
  - emergent vision-language capabilities (cite): write code from images, plots -> Markdown tables, web browsing
- Bridging modules
  - two aspects: transform/align visual tokens to LLM format; use transformed tokens
- Transformation and alignment
  - Flamingo (cite), BLIP-2 (cite): Perceiver-Resampler/Q-Former; flexible, nuanced alignment; more compute, possible information loss (cite)
  - LLaVA, MiniGPT-v2: simpler MLP; less compute, fewer learnable params; may miss intricacies of visual data
- Integration
  - Flamingo-style: cross-attention, no longer token sequence, manages compute
  - LLaVA-style: direct concatenation, simple but longer sequence, more compute
- Resolution
  - both use low resolution because of pretrained ViT encoders (cite)
  - fine for image-level semantics, not region-level detail
  - recent efforts toward higher resolution (cite)
  - compute grows quadratically with sequence length; 224\times 224 (cite) to 448\times 448 = 16 times self-attention compute
- InfiMM-HD
  - merges Flamingo and LLaVA styles
  - MLP for transformation/alignment (like LLaVA): efficiency + precise processing
  - cross-attention for integration (like Flamingo): avoids long sequences
  - high-res input in Flamingo-style MLLMs still emerging; pioneering
  - four training stages:
    - 224\times 224 pretraining for alignment
    - continued pretraining, interpolated positional embeddings, 448\times 448, multiple datasets, LLM frozen
    - full resolution, resized to nearest multiple of 448\times 448, 2D positional embeddings, cropped to subimages
    - visual instruction fine-tuning: vision encoder frozen, LLM trainable
- Contributions
  - InfiMM-HD: MLP alignment + Flamingo-style cross-attention; high-res inputs
  - four-stage pipeline with reduced training cost
  - benchmarks show visual perception proficiency; ablations show design superiority among cross-attention-style models

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have changed a lot by combining pretrained vision encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs), and we can see this trend in Flamingo, BLIP-2, LLaVA, MiniGPT-4 and etc. MLLMs can show emergent vision-language capabilities. For example, they use the single-modal capabilities of the pretrained vision encoders and LLMs together, so they can write code based on images, turn plots in images into tables in Markdown format, and do web browsing.

To combine pretrained vision encoders and LLMs well in MLLMs, you need well designed vision-language bridging modules. These modules deal with two important things: transforming and aligning the visual tokens into a format the LLM can use, and then using these transformed tokens.

For transforming and aligning visual tokens, models like Flamingo and BLIP-2 use Perceiver-Resampler/Q-Former techniques. These are flexible and give nuanced alignment with the language tokens, but they need more computation and can lose information. On the other hand, models like LLaVA and MiniGPT-v2 use simpler Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) approaches. This reduces the computational complexity and the number of learnable parameters, but it may not capture all the details of the visual data.

Integrating the visual and language tokens is just as important. Flamingo-style architectures use cross-attention, which lets the two types of tokens interact in detail without making the token sequence longer, so the computational load is handled efficiently. LLaVA-style models instead just concatenate the tokens directly, which is simple but makes the token sequence longer and the computation more complex.

- Resolution
  - both architectures low resolution due to pretrained ViT encoders
  - enough for image-level semantics, not region-level detail
  - recent high-res efforts; compute quadratic in sequence length; 224\times 224 -> 448\times 448 = 16 times self-attention
- InfiMM-HD
  - MLP alignment like LLaVA; cross-attention integration like Flamingo
  - high-res in Flamingo-style MLLMs still emerging; pioneering
  - four stages: 224\times 224 pretraining; 448\times 448 continued pretraining, interpolated pos. embeddings, LLM frozen; full resolution, multiple of 448\times 448, 2D pos. embeddings, subimages; instruction fine-tuning, vision encoder frozen
- Contributions: architecture; four-stage pipeline, reduced cost; benchmarks + ablations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have changed a lot by combining pretrained vision encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs), and we can see this trend in Flamingo, BLIP-2, LLaVA, MiniGPT-4 and etc. MLLMs can show emergent vision-language capabilities. For example, they use the single-modal capabilities of the pretrained vision encoders and LLMs together, so they can write code based on images, turn plots in images into tables in Markdown format, and do web browsing.

To combine pretrained vision encoders and LLMs well in MLLMs, you need well designed vision-language bridging modules. These modules deal with two important things: transforming and aligning the visual tokens into a format the LLM can use, and then using these transformed tokens.

For transforming and aligning visual tokens, models like Flamingo and BLIP-2 use Perceiver-Resampler/Q-Former techniques. These are flexible and give nuanced alignment with the language tokens, but they need more computation and can lose information. On the other hand, models like LLaVA and MiniGPT-v2 use simpler Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) approaches. This reduces the computational complexity and the number of learnable parameters, but it may not capture all the details of the visual data.

Integrating the visual and language tokens is just as important. Flamingo-style architectures use cross-attention, which lets the two types of tokens interact in detail without making the token sequence longer, so the computational load is handled efficiently. LLaVA-style models instead just concatenate the tokens directly, which is simple but makes the token sequence longer and the computation more complex.

Although they are different, both architectures use low image resolution because of the pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders. Low resolution is enough for basic image-level semantic understanding but not for detailed region-level analysis. Some recent efforts try to make MLLMs handle higher-resolution images. But there are still big challenges, mainly because the computation tends to grow quadratically with the sequence length for larger images. For example, going from 224\times 224 image resolution to 448\times 448 makes the self-attention computation 16 times larger.

To deal with these challenges we introduce InfiMM-HD, a new MLLM architecture for processing high-resolution images. InfiMM-HD combines methods from both Flamingo-style and LLaVA-style MLLMs. For transformation and alignment it uses an MLP-based approach like LLaVA, which transforms and aligns visual tokens into formats the LLM can use. This balances computational efficiency and precise processing. For integration, InfiMM-HD uses a cross-attention mechanism like Flamingo-style MLLMs to combine the visual token features with the language tokens. This avoids the computational problems with longer token sequences mentioned above. High-resolution image input for Flamingo-style MLLMs is still an emerging research area, and InfiMM-HD is a significant, pioneering step in it, taking the best of both approaches to improve MLLM performance with high-resolution visual inputs.

The pretrained vision encoders have resolution limits, so to get around them InfiMM-HD is trained in four stages that improve resolution handling while keeping vision-language alignment. First, the model is pretrained on 224\times 224 images for efficient visual-language alignment. Then it continues pretraining on 448\times 448 images from multiple datasets with interpolated positional embeddings, with the LLMs frozen. After that it is trained with full-resolution images, which are resized to the nearest multiple of 448\times 448, given 2D positional embeddings and cropped into multiple subimages. In the last stage the model does visual instruction fine-tuning, where the vision encoder is frozen and the LLM is trainable, to improve instruction-following. This training approach is important for how well the model adapts and performs with different input resolutions. Our contributions are:

- We present InfiMM-HD, a new MLLM that uses an MLP-based approach to transform and align visual tokens, together with a Flamingo-style cross-attention mechanism to integrate the transformed visual tokens and the language tokens in a better and efficient way. It is designed to process high-resolution image inputs seamlessly.

- We present a four-stage training pipeline that gets a high-resolution Multimodal Large Language Model with lower training cost. It goes from an initial low-resolution pretraining stage, to a continue pretraining stage for knowledge injection and alignment, to a dynamic resolution adaption stage for high resolution, and finally to a visual instruction fine-tuning stage.

- Experiments on diverse benchmarks show that our model is very good at visual perception. Ablation studies also show that our design is better within cross-attention-style Multimodal Language Model architectures.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The landscape of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has been transformed by integrating pretrained vision encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs) [1,2,3], a trend exemplified by Flamingo [4], BLIP-2 [5], LLaVA [6], MiniGPT-4 [7] and etc. MLLMs can exhibit emergent vision-language capabilities [8]. For example, by leveraging the combined single-modal capabilities of pretrained vision encoders and LLMs, they can write code according to images, convert plots in images into Markdown format tables, and perform web browsing.

Effectively integrating pretrained vision encoders with Large Language Models in MLLMs relies on carefully designed vision-language bridging modules. These modules address two critical aspects: transforming and aligning visual tokens into LLM-compatible formats, and subsequently utilizing these transformed tokens.

For the transformation and alignment of visual tokens, models such as Flamingo [4] and BLIP-2 [5] employ Perceiver-Resampler/Q-Former techniques, which offer flexibility and nuanced alignment with language counterparts but come with higher computational demands and potential information loss [9]. Conversely, models such as LLaVA and MiniGPT-v2 take a different route, using simpler Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) approaches. This reduces computational complexity and the number of learnable parameters, but it might not capture the full intricacies of visual data.

The integration of visual and language tokens is equally vital. Flamingo-style architectures employ cross-attention mechanisms, enabling intricate interactions between token types without expanding the token sequence length, which manages the computational load efficiently. LLaVA-style models, however, use direct concatenation, which is straightforward but increases token sequence length and computational complexity.

Though different, both architectures use low image resolution due to pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders [10,11,12]. Low resolution suffices for basic image-level semantic understanding but falls short for detailed, region-level analysis. Recent efforts [13,14,15] aim to let MLLMs handle higher-resolution images. However, significant challenges remain, mainly because computational demands increase quadratically with sequence length for larger images. For instance, increasing the image resolution from 224\times 224 [16] to 448\times 448 multiplies the self-attention computation by 16 times.

To address these challenges, we introduce InfiMM-HD, an innovative MLLM architecture designed for processing high-resolution images. InfiMM-HD merges methodologies from both Flamingo-style and LLaVA-style MLLMs. For the transformation and alignment phase, it adopts an MLP-based approach, akin to LLaVA, effectively transforming and aligning visual tokens into LLM-compatible formats. This strategy balances computational efficiency with precise processing. In the integration phase, InfiMM-HD uses a cross-attention mechanism, reminiscent of Flamingo-style MLLMs, to incorporate visual token features with language tokens. This mitigates the computational challenges of longer token sequences mentioned above. Notably, while high-resolution image input for Flamingo-style MLLMs is still an emerging area of research, InfiMM-HD marks a significant, pioneering advance in this domain, blending the best of both worlds to improve MLLM performance with high-resolution visual inputs.

To overcome the resolution constraints of pretrained vision encoders, InfiMM-HD is trained in four stages, improving resolution handling while maintaining vision-language alignment. First, the model is pretrained with 224\times 224 resolution images for efficient visual-language alignment. It then continues pretraining with interpolated positional embeddings on 448\times 448 images from multiple datasets, keeping the LLMs frozen. Next, it is trained with full-resolution images, resized to the nearest multiple of 448\times 448, with added 2D positional embeddings and cropped into multiple subimages. In the final stage, the model undergoes visual instruction fine-tuning, with the vision encoder frozen and the LLM trainable to enhance instruction-following capability. This structured training approach is crucial for the model's adaptability and performance across input resolutions. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We present InfiMM-HD, a pioneering MLLM that employs an MLP-based approach for visual token transformation and alignment, coupled with a Flamingo-style cross-attention mechanism for enhanced and efficient integration of transformed visual and language tokens. It is designed to seamlessly process high-resolution image inputs.

- • We present a four-stage training pipeline that achieves a high-resolution Multimodal Large Language Model with reduced training cost, from an initial low-resolution pretraining stage, to a continue pretraining stage for knowledge injection and alignment, to a dynamic resolution adaption stage for high resolution adoption, and finally a visual instruction fine-tuning stage.

- • Experiments across diverse benchmarks show the remarkable proficiency of our model in visual perception. Additionally, comprehensive ablation studies underscore the superiority of our design among cross-attention-style Multimodal Language Model architectures.
